Questions to Ask Yourself

  • Which rooms do you photograph and save most often — and what do they have in common?
  • What materials make you feel calm: raw wood, polished marble, natural linen, painted metal?
  • Do you gravitate towards pattern or towards plain surfaces?
  • Are you drawn to warmth and texture, or to clean lines and negative space?
  • When you've decorated a room you loved, what were the two or three things that made it feel right?
  • Which styles do you keep circling even when you try something new — bohemian, Scandi, industrial, traditional?

I once worked with a client who was convinced she had no consistent taste because her Pinterest boards looked "all over the place." When we sat down and mapped her saves, almost every image featured exposed natural wood, organic shapes and a warm, dusty colour palette. She was actually a natural maximalist with a Japandi soul — she just hadn't seen it that way. Once we named it, her shopping decisions became so much easier.

Pro Tip: Print out or screenshot ten rooms you genuinely love. Line them up and look for what they share — not the style label, but the actual visual qualities: warmth, texture, scale, colour temperature. That overlap is your style DNA.

How to Find Unifying Elements That Tie Mixed Styles Together

Once you know your style DNA, the next job is finding the connective tissue between your chosen aesthetics. Unifying elements are the quiet things in a room that make everything feel like it belongs together, even when individual pieces come from completely different design traditions.

The three most reliable unifying elements are colour, texture and material. If your sofa is mid-century, your rug is Moroccan and your shelving is industrial, a shared warm bronze tone running through cushions, lamp bases and picture frames will pull the whole thing together more effectively than trying to "match" styles.

[[IMG|unifying-elements-mixed-style-room|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Three Unifying Elements for Mixed-Style Rooms", then a clear visual comparison showing three labelled columns side by side: Column 1 labelled "Colour" with a swatch strip showing a warm terracotta-to-cream palette; Column 2 labelled "Texture" with small sketched icons of linen, rattan and velvet; Column 3 labelled "Material" with icons of wood grain, matte metal and stone. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Key Unifying Elements to Work With

  • Colour palette: Choose two or three anchor colours that appear in every room in some form — on walls, cushions, decor objects or art.
  • Material family: Repeat one or two materials across different pieces — natural oak, matte black metal, aged brass, raw linen.
  • Texture balance: Make sure every room has a mix of smooth and rough, shiny and matte — this creates cohesion even when styles clash.
  • Scale consistency: Keep furniture proportions in a similar range so no single piece feels wildly out of place.
  • Finish temperature: Warm finishes (brass, amber glass, honey wood) mix better together than warm and cool finishes thrown in at random.
Pro Tip: Hold a swatch card against each major furniture piece in the room. If they all share at least one colour value — even a very subtle one — your eye will read them as a family. If none of them share anything, that's where the disconnect is coming from.
[[PRODUCT|natural rattan pendant light for eclectic living room]]

Room-by-Room Audit Checklist for Blending Styles Cohesively

Mixing styles works best when you audit each room individually rather than trying to solve the whole house at once. A room-by-room approach lets you identify exactly where the friction is and fix it without touching what's already working.

I'd suggest walking through each room with fresh eyes — ideally after a short break so you're not "blind" to it — and working through a simple checklist. The goal is to spot where the room feels jarring and why.

[[IMG|room-by-room-audit-checklist-blending-styles|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A calm, light-filled kitchen-diner where a mix of styles is evident: a Shaker-style painted dresser sits alongside a concrete-topped island and industrial bar stools. A Black British man in his forties stands with a notepad, looking at the room carefully and making notes, as if doing an assessment of the space.]]

Room Audit Checklist

  • Colour count: How many distinct colours are competing in this room? Aim for no more than three anchor colours plus neutrals.
  • Style count: How many different style references are present? Two or three is fine; five or more usually needs editing.
  • Focal point check: Is there one clear thing your eye lands on first, or does the room feel directionless?
  • Material repeat: Does the same material (wood tone, metal finish) appear at least twice in the room?
  • Scale check: Is anything dramatically larger or smaller than everything else in a way that feels wrong rather than intentional?
  • Wall review: Do the walls (art, colour, decor) feel connected to the furniture below, or are they a completely separate world?
  • Negative space: Is there anywhere the eye can rest, or is every surface covered?

When I work with clients on this, the most common find in the wall review is that the furniture and the wall treatment are ignoring each other completely. The furniture might be warm-toned and organic, but the wall art is cool and graphic — and those two worlds haven't been introduced to each other yet. That's usually the quickest fix in the room.

Real Example: A client's dining room had a beautiful antique table, modern chairs and a bold geometric rug — but the walls were bare. Once we added a warm abstract print in a tonal terracotta that picked up the rug's rust tones, the whole room suddenly made sense. The art was the missing introduction between old and new.
[[PRODUCT|abstract terracotta wall art prints for dining room]]

How to Shop for Decor Pieces That Bridge Two or More Design Styles

Shopping for a mixed-style home is actually one of the more enjoyable parts of the process — once you know what to look for. The pieces that bridge two or more aesthetics tend to share a few specific qualities, and once you can spot them, they jump out at you in shops and online.

The best bridging pieces are usually the ones that feel slightly outside a single category. A hand-thrown ceramic vase in a matte finish, for example, works in a Scandi room, a bohemian room and a contemporary room. It doesn't belong exclusively to any one style, so it fits into all of them.

[[IMG|shopping-for-decor-that-bridges-design-styles|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A flatlay-style overhead shot of a wooden table surface arranged with carefully chosen decor bridging objects: a matte black ceramic vase, a small woven rattan tray, a smooth stone object, a sprig of dried pampas grass, and a folded piece of warm linen fabric in ochre. A mixed-heritage woman in her late twenties reaches into frame with one hand, arranging the objects thoughtfully.]]

What Makes a Piece a Good Style Bridge?

  • Natural materials: Wood, stone, ceramic, linen and rattan tend to feel at home in almost any style context.
  • Neutral or earthy tones: Pieces in warm whites, sand, terracotta, slate or warm grey work across a wide range of aesthetics.
  • Handmade quality: Slight irregularity (a hand-thrown pot, a woven edge) adds warmth without being style-specific.
  • Simple silhouettes: Clean shapes that don't shout a single era are the easiest to place in multiple contexts.
  • Matte or low-sheen finishes: These tend to feel less "designed" and more universal than high-gloss pieces.
Pro Tip: When you're unsure whether a piece will work in your mixed-style room, hold it against your unifying colour card. If it shares at least one tone with your palette, it almost certainly works. If it fights every tone, leave it behind.
[[PRODUCT|handwoven jute rug for eclectic living space]]

Specific Wall Art Strategies for Anchoring a Mixed-Style Room

Wall art is arguably the single most powerful tool you have when mixing multiple interior design styles, because it sits at eye level and draws everything in the room into a conversation with it. The right piece doesn't just decorate the wall — it acts as the room's editor, telling you what matters and what supports it.

The strategy I use most often is what I call the "bridge print" approach: choosing one large artwork that contains at least two of the colours and at least one of the textures present in the room. That one piece does the heavy lifting of visually connecting a sofa from one style world to a rug from another.

[[IMG|wall-art-anchoring-mixed-style-room|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, warm tones with both industrial and bohemian style references visible. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A living room showing a deliberate mix of a dark metal industrial shelving unit alongside a low rattan sofa draped with a cream textured throw. A large woven macramé wall hanging is positioned centrally above the sofa, with a ceramic vase and a trailing plant on the shelf. A white British woman in her late thirties stands beside the shelving unit, turning towards the sofa with her head tilted slightly, studying the arrangement.]]

Wall Art Anchoring Strategies

  • The bridge print: One large artwork that contains colours from both style worlds in the room — this visually links them.
  • The gallery wall mix: Combine frames of the same metal finish but different styles of art — one botanical, one abstract, one line drawing — for an intentionally eclectic look that still feels controlled.
  • The texture anchor: Use a textile wall piece (macramé, woven tapestry, fabric art) to bring warmth and softness to a room that skews industrial or contemporary.
  • The contrast statement: In a traditional room, one bold contemporary artwork creates deliberate, confident contrast — it reads as a choice rather than a mistake.
  • The tonal print series: Three prints in the same colour family but different subjects bridge multiple styles by keeping colour consistent while varying content.
[[PRODUCT|large abstract wall art print for living room focal point]]
Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether your wall art is anchoring the room or floating away from it, cut a piece of brown paper the same size as the artwork and tape it to the wall for a day. Live with the scale before you commit. Scale mistakes are the number one reason a piece feels wrong even when the style is right.

Visual Hierarchy and Focal Point Creation Using Art in Eclectic Spaces

One of the reasons eclectic rooms can feel chaotic is that there's no clear focal point — the eye doesn't know where to land first, so it bounces around and gets tired. Creating a visual hierarchy using art is one of the most effective ways to give an eclectic room a sense of calm authority.

Think of visual hierarchy as a simple conversation: there's one thing that speaks loudest, two or three things that respond to it, and everything else that plays a supporting role. Your wall art should almost always be the thing that speaks loudest, especially in a mixed-style space where furniture can't make that decision by itself.

[[IMG|visual-hierarchy-focal-point-eclectic-room|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Creating Visual Hierarchy with Wall Art". Below, a simple top-down room diagram showing a living room layout with three layers labelled: "Layer 1 — Hero Art (largest, eye lands here first)", "Layer 2 — Supporting Decor (medium scale, responds to art)", "Layer 3 — Background Elements (small scale, texture and fill)". Arrows indicate the visual flow from layer 1 downward. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

How to Create a Strong Focal Point

  • Choose one wall as your "hero wall" — usually the one facing the entry point into the room.
  • Place your largest or most visually dominant artwork at eye level on that wall, centred or deliberately off-centre with intention.
  • Let the furniture arrangement respond to the art — angle seating towards it, or balance shelving on either side.
  • Keep the other walls quieter: smaller pieces, mirrors or simple wall sconces rather than competing large-scale art.
  • Use lighting (a picture light, a directional spot) to reinforce the focal point after dark.
Real Example: I once helped a client whose eclectic sitting room felt permanently unsettled. She had art on every wall at roughly the same scale — nothing led the eye. We moved everything off three walls, placed one large botanical print on the chimney breast and let the room breathe. The difference was immediate. The other walls got one mirror and one shelf arrangement, and suddenly the room felt curated.
[[PRODUCT|oversized botanical wall art prints for chimney breast]]

Style Pairing Guides: Which Aesthetics Work Best Together

Not all styles mix with equal ease. Some pairings feel natural almost immediately; others take more work to reconcile. Understanding which aesthetics share common ground makes the whole process much less stressful.

Below is a practical pairing guide based on what I've seen work consistently in real homes — not theoretical combinations, but actual rooms that land well.

[[IMG|style-pairing-guide-mixed-interiors|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Style Pairing Guide: Which Aesthetics Mix Well". Below, four rows of two-column comparisons, each showing two style labels connected by a "+" symbol, with a one-line note on their shared common ground: Row 1: "Modern + Bohemian — shared: organic shapes, earthy tones"; Row 2: "Industrial + Scandinavian — shared: muted palette, raw materials"; Row 3: "Traditional + Contemporary — shared: quality craft, symmetry"; Row 4: "Japandi + Coastal — shared: natural materials, calm palette". Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]
Style Pairing What They Share Wall Art That Bridges Them
Modern + Bohemian Organic forms, earthy palette Abstract organic prints, botanical line art
Industrial + Scandinavian Raw materials, muted tones, function Minimalist black-and-white photography, architectural prints
Traditional + Contemporary Quality craft, symmetry, restraint Classic subjects in a modern palette, portrait-inspired abstract art
Japandi + Coastal Natural materials, calm palette, texture Soft watercolour landscapes, neutral coastal prints
Maximalist + Art Deco Pattern, richness, confident colour Bold geometric prints, jewel-toned abstract art

The pairings that cause the most friction in practice tend to be rustic farmhouse with sleek ultra-modern, or very ornate traditional with stark minimalism. They can be done, but they need a very strong unifying element — usually a consistent colour palette — to keep them from fighting each other.

Pro Tip: When pairing styles, start with the two that share the most in common — usually material or colour — and treat the third or fourth style as an accent rather than an equal partner. Let one style dominate at about 60%, the second at 30%, and accent styles at 10%.
[[PRODUCT|minimalist black and white photography prints for industrial Scandi room]]

How to Use a Consistent Colour Palette to Unify Clashing Furniture Styles

Colour is genuinely the most powerful unifying tool you have when mixing multiple interior design styles. A consistent palette can make a Victorian armchair and a 1970s arc floor lamp look completely intentional together. Without it, even beautifully individual pieces can feel like strangers at a party.

The approach I recommend is what I call the "60-30-10 palette rule" — not a new idea, but one that's particularly useful in mixed-style rooms. Sixty percent of the room is your dominant colour (usually a neutral), thirty percent is a secondary colour (usually a mid-tone), and ten percent is an accent that ties everything together.

[[IMG|consistent-colour-palette-unify-furniture-styles|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette with warm terracotta and sage green accents. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A sitting room where clearly different furniture styles are unified by a consistent warm palette: a Victorian carved wooden chair reupholstered in sage velvet, a 1970s-inspired arc floor lamp in brass, a contemporary low linen sofa in warm cream, and terracotta ceramic pots on a shelf. A Latin American woman in her fifties stands at the edge of the room holding a colour-swatch card, comparing it to a cushion on the sofa.]]

How to Build Your Unifying Colour Palette

  • Pull two or three colours from the piece you love most and can't change (often a rug, a sofa or a feature wall).
  • Use those colours as your filter for every other buying decision in the room.
  • Repeat each palette colour at least three times in the room — in art, cushions, decor objects, plant pots.
  • Use your accent colour on at least one piece of wall art or wall decor so the walls feel connected to the room below.
  • If two furniture pieces are fighting each other, add a cushion or throw in a colour that appears in both — it acts as a visual translator.

Here's a fix I use all the time: I had a client with a deep navy velvet sofa and a warm oak mid-century coffee table that felt completely at odds. We added a warm-toned abstract print that had both dusty navy and amber in it, two terracotta cushions on the sofa and a small amber glass vase on the table. That's all it took. Same furniture, completely different feel.

Pro Tip: If you're stuck on your palette, take your phone to each room and photograph it. View the photos in black and white. If the values (lights and darks) feel balanced in greyscale, the room has a good tonal structure regardless of which colours are fighting. If it looks patchy or too dark in one corner, that's where your colour balance needs work.
[[PRODUCT|warm abstract wall art with terracotta and navy tones]]

Common Mixing Mistakes to Avoid and How to Fix Them

The mistakes I see most often in mixed-style rooms are remarkably consistent — and the good news is they're all fixable without starting again from scratch. Most of them come down to a few specific missteps that are easy to spot once you know what to look for.

I'll be honest: I've made a couple of these mistakes myself in rooms I've styled early in my career. The "too many focal points" problem in particular caught me out in a client's bedroom where I was genuinely delighted with every individual piece — and then we stepped back and realised the room looked like an auction house.

[[IMG|common-mixing-mistakes-interior-design|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A tidy, well-resolved bedroom showing a confident mix of rustic and contemporary styles done correctly: a raw linen bedhead, a concrete-finish bedside table, warm wooden flooring, a simple rattan pendant and a trailing pothos plant on a shelf. A Black British woman in her mid-thirties stands in the doorway of the bedroom, arms crossed and smiling at the resolved, calm room.]]

Common Mistakes and Their Fixes

  • Mistake: Too many focal points. Fix: Choose one hero element per room and subordinate everything else to it.
  • Mistake: Mixing too many metal finishes. Fix: Pick two finishes maximum — one warm, one dark — and repeat them consistently.
  • Mistake: Scale inconsistency. Fix: Ensure your largest pieces are genuinely large and your small pieces genuinely small — avoid the mid-sized "nothing" zone.
  • Mistake: Art that doesn't connect to the room. Fix: Choose art that contains at least one colour from your room palette.
  • Mistake: All styles equally weighted. Fix: Let one style dominate and use others as accents. A 60/30/10 split always reads as more intentional.
  • Mistake: Ignoring the floor. Fix: Your rug is effectively the ground on which all styles meet — treat it as a unifier, not an afterthought.
  • Mistake: Bare walls in an eclectic room. Fix: In a mixed-style space, bare walls don't read as minimal — they read as unfinished. Even one piece of considered wall art changes this entirely.
Real Example: The mistake I always see with gallery walls in mixed-style rooms is mixing too many frame colours. Gold, black, white and natural wood all in one arrangement is a lot to manage. Choose one frame colour — I usually recommend matte black or natural oak — and let the art itself be the variety. You'll get all the eclectic energy with none of the chaos.

More About Mixing Interior Design Styles the Right Way

Understanding the history and logic behind how different design eras interact helps you make bolder, more confident decisions when blending aesthetics.

One thing I find genuinely useful to remind clients is that mixing styles has always been the norm, not the exception, in well-loved homes. Historically, homes accumulated pieces across decades — a grandmother's armchair here, a contemporary lamp there — and it was the sense of personal history that made them feel alive. The design world's push towards "complete looks" is a relatively recent commercial idea, not a design principle. If you want to go deeper on how different design eras can be combined thoughtfully, This Is the Correct Way to Mix Design Eras is a really solid read that backs this up with practical examples.

The most important thing I'd add is that mixing styles successfully is a skill you develop with practice, not something that has to be perfect from the first attempt. Start with one room, get that feeling right, and let the confidence carry you forward.

WATCH: Master the Art of Mixing Interior Design Styles

Ready to Make Your Mixed-Style Home Work for You?

If there's one thing I hope you take away from all of this, it's that loving multiple interior design styles is not a problem to solve — it's actually a real advantage. The most interesting homes I've ever walked into have always been the ones that reflect a genuine human being with real, layered tastes, not a showroom built around a single aesthetic.

Start small. Pick one room, identify your two dominant styles, find your unifying colour and choose one piece of wall art that bridges them. You don't have to transform the whole house this weekend.

So tell me — which two styles are you trying to bring together right now, and what's the one piece in your room that you absolutely refuse to get rid of? I'd love to hear what you're working with.

Mixing multiple interior design styles is not just allowed — it's actually one of the most interesting ways to create a home that feels genuinely personal. The key is knowing which elements to use as a through-line so the room reads as curated rather than confused. With the right approach to colour, texture, wall art and decor, you can pull together two, three or even four distinct aesthetics and make them feel completely at home with each other.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in your living room, looked at the mid-century sofa you love, the rustic wooden sideboard you couldn't leave behind, and the abstract print on the wall — and thought, "Does any of this actually go together?" You're not alone. I hear this from almost every client I work with, and the good news is that the right wall art choices alone can do more to unify a mixed-style space than almost any other single decision.

Quick answer: You can successfully mix multiple interior design styles by identifying a shared colour palette, choosing unifying materials and textures, and anchoring each room with a considered piece of wall art or decor that bridges your chosen aesthetics. The result is an eclectic space that feels intentional rather than accidental.

Mixing styles is sometimes called eclectic decorating, but that word can feel a bit vague. What it really means in practice is finding the common thread — a warm wood tone, a muted earthy palette, a repeated geometric shape — and letting that thread run through every decision you make. If you're looking for unique wall art or unique home decor that genuinely bridges two or more aesthetics, it's worth starting with your own style DNA before you shop.

How to Identify Your Personal Style DNA Across Multiple Design Aesthetics

Before you can mix styles confidently, you need to know which ones genuinely speak to you — not just which ones look good on Instagram. Your personal style DNA is the combination of aesthetics you keep returning to, even when you try to talk yourself out of them.

Start by looking at what you already own and love. Not what you bought because it was on sale, or because a magazine said it was trending — but the pieces that have moved with you from flat to flat and that you'd genuinely be upset to lose.

Questions to Ask Yourself

  • Which rooms do you photograph and save most often — and what do they have in common?
  • What materials make you feel calm: raw wood, polished marble, natural linen, painted metal?
  • Do you gravitate towards pattern or towards plain surfaces?
  • Are you drawn to warmth and texture, or to clean lines and negative space?
  • When you've decorated a room you loved, what were the two or three things that made it feel right?
  • Which styles do you keep circling even when you try something new — bohemian, Scandi, industrial, traditional?

I once worked with a client who was convinced she had no consistent taste because her Pinterest boards looked "all over the place." When we sat down and mapped her saves, almost every image featured exposed natural wood, organic shapes and a warm, dusty colour palette. She was actually a natural maximalist with a Japandi soul — she just hadn't seen it that way. Once we named it, her shopping decisions became so much easier.

Pro Tip: Print out or screenshot ten rooms you genuinely love. Line them up and look for what they share — not the style label, but the actual visual qualities: warmth, texture, scale, colour temperature. That overlap is your style DNA.

How to Find Unifying Elements That Tie Mixed Styles Together

Once you know your style DNA, the next job is finding the connective tissue between your chosen aesthetics. Unifying elements are the quiet things in a room that make everything feel like it belongs together, even when individual pieces come from completely different design traditions.

The three most reliable unifying elements are colour, texture and material. If your sofa is mid-century, your rug is Moroccan and your shelving is industrial, a shared warm bronze tone running through cushions, lamp bases and picture frames will pull the whole thing together more effectively than trying to "match" styles.

Key Unifying Elements to Work With

  • Colour palette: Choose two or three anchor colours that appear in every room in some form — on walls, cushions, decor objects or art.
  • Material family: Repeat one or two materials across different pieces — natural oak, matte black metal, aged brass, raw linen.
  • Texture balance: Make sure every room has a mix of smooth and rough, shiny and matte — this creates cohesion even when styles clash.
  • Scale consistency: Keep furniture proportions in a similar range so no single piece feels wildly out of place.
  • Finish temperature: Warm finishes (brass, amber glass, honey wood) mix better together than warm and cool finishes thrown in at random.
Pro Tip: Hold a swatch card against each major furniture piece in the room. If they all share at least one colour value — even a very subtle one — your eye will read them as a family. If none of them share anything, that's where the disconnect is coming from.

Room-by-Room Audit Checklist for Blending Styles Cohesively

Mixing styles works best when you audit each room individually rather than trying to solve the whole house at once. A room-by-room approach lets you identify exactly where the friction is and fix it without touching what's already working.

I'd suggest walking through each room with fresh eyes — ideally after a short break so you're not "blind" to it — and working through a simple checklist. The goal is to spot where the room feels jarring and why.

Room Audit Checklist

  • Colour count: How many distinct colours are competing in this room? Aim for no more than three anchor colours plus neutrals.
  • Style count: How many different style references are present? Two or three is fine; five or more usually needs editing.
  • Focal point check: Is there one clear thing your eye lands on first, or does the room feel directionless?
  • Material repeat: Does the same material (wood tone, metal finish) appear at least twice in the room?
  • Scale check: Is anything dramatically larger or smaller than everything else in a way that feels wrong rather than intentional?
  • Wall review: Do the walls (art, colour, decor) feel connected to the furniture below, or are they a completely separate world?
  • Negative space: Is there anywhere the eye can rest, or is every surface covered?

When I work with clients on this, the most common find in the wall review is that the furniture and the wall treatment are ignoring each other completely. The furniture might be warm-toned and organic, but the wall art is cool and graphic — and those two worlds haven't been introduced to each other yet. That's usually the quickest fix in the room.

Real Example: A client's dining room had a beautiful antique table, modern chairs and a bold geometric rug — but the walls were bare. Once we added a warm abstract print in a tonal terracotta that picked up the rug's rust tones, the whole room suddenly made sense. The art was the missing introduction between old and new.

How to Shop for Decor Pieces That Bridge Two or More Design Styles

Shopping for a mixed-style home is actually one of the more enjoyable parts of the process — once you know what to look for. The pieces that bridge two or more aesthetics tend to share a few specific qualities, and once you can spot them, they jump out at you in shops and online.

The best bridging pieces are usually the ones that feel slightly outside a single category. A hand-thrown ceramic vase in a matte finish, for example, works in a Scandi room, a bohemian room and a contemporary room. It doesn't belong exclusively to any one style, so it fits into all of them.

What Makes a Piece a Good Style Bridge?

  • Natural materials: Wood, stone, ceramic, linen and rattan tend to feel at home in almost any style context.
  • Neutral or earthy tones: Pieces in warm whites, sand, terracotta, slate or warm grey work across a wide range of aesthetics.
  • Handmade quality: Slight irregularity (a hand-thrown pot, a woven edge) adds warmth without being style-specific.
  • Simple silhouettes: Clean shapes that don't shout a single era are the easiest to place in multiple contexts.
  • Matte or low-sheen finishes: These tend to feel less "designed" and more universal than high-gloss pieces.
Pro Tip: When you're unsure whether a piece will work in your mixed-style room, hold it against your unifying colour card. If it shares at least one tone with your palette, it almost certainly works. If it fights every tone, leave it behind.

Specific Wall Art Strategies for Anchoring a Mixed-Style Room

Wall art is arguably the single most powerful tool you have when mixing multiple interior design styles, because it sits at eye level and draws everything in the room into a conversation with it. The right piece doesn't just decorate the wall — it acts as the room's editor, telling you what matters and what supports it.

The strategy I use most often is what I call the "bridge print" approach: choosing one large artwork that contains at least two of the colours and at least one of the textures present in the room. That one piece does the heavy lifting of visually connecting a sofa from one style world to a rug from another.

Wall Art Anchoring Strategies

  • The bridge print: One large artwork that contains colours from both style worlds in the room — this visually links them.
  • The gallery wall mix: Combine frames of the same metal finish but different styles of art — one botanical, one abstract, one line drawing — for an intentionally eclectic look that still feels controlled.
  • The texture anchor: Use a textile wall piece (macramé, woven tapestry, fabric art) to bring warmth and softness to a room that skews industrial or contemporary.
  • The contrast statement: In a traditional room, one bold contemporary artwork creates deliberate, confident contrast — it reads as a choice rather than a mistake.
  • The tonal print series: Three prints in the same colour family but different subjects bridge multiple styles by keeping colour consistent while varying content.

Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether your wall art is anchoring the room or floating away from it, cut a piece of brown paper the same size as the artwork and tape it to the wall for a day. Live with the scale before you commit. Scale mistakes are the number one reason a piece feels wrong even when the style is right.

Visual Hierarchy and Focal Point Creation Using Art in Eclectic Spaces

One of the reasons eclectic rooms can feel chaotic is that there's no clear focal point — the eye doesn't know where to land first, so it bounces around and gets tired. Creating a visual hierarchy using art is one of the most effective ways to give an eclectic room a sense of calm authority.

Think of visual hierarchy as a simple conversation: there's one thing that speaks loudest, two or three things that respond to it, and everything else that plays a supporting role. Your wall art should almost always be the thing that speaks loudest, especially in a mixed-style space where furniture can't make that decision by itself.

How to Create a Strong Focal Point

  • Choose one wall as your "hero wall" — usually the one facing the entry point into the room.
  • Place your largest or most visually dominant artwork at eye level on that wall, centred or deliberately off-centre with intention.
  • Let the furniture arrangement respond to the art — angle seating towards it, or balance shelving on either side.
  • Keep the other walls quieter: smaller pieces, mirrors or simple wall sconces rather than competing large-scale art.
  • Use lighting (a picture light, a directional spot) to reinforce the focal point after dark.
Real Example: I once helped a client whose eclectic sitting room felt permanently unsettled. She had art on every wall at roughly the same scale — nothing led the eye. We moved everything off three walls, placed one large botanical print on the chimney breast and let the room breathe. The difference was immediate. The other walls got one mirror and one shelf arrangement, and suddenly the room felt curated.

Style Pairing Guides: Which Aesthetics Work Best Together

Not all styles mix with equal ease. Some pairings feel natural almost immediately; others take more work to reconcile. Understanding which aesthetics share common ground makes the whole process much less stressful.

Below is a practical pairing guide based on what I've seen work consistently in real homes — not theoretical combinations, but actual rooms that land well.

Style Pairing What They Share Wall Art That Bridges Them
Modern + Bohemian Organic forms, earthy palette Abstract organic prints, botanical line art
Industrial + Scandinavian Raw materials, muted tones, function Minimalist black-and-white photography, architectural prints
Traditional + Contemporary Quality craft, symmetry, restraint Classic subjects in a modern palette, portrait-inspired abstract art
Japandi + Coastal Natural materials, calm palette, texture Soft watercolour landscapes, neutral coastal prints
Maximalist + Art Deco Pattern, richness, confident colour Bold geometric prints, jewel-toned abstract art

The pairings that cause the most friction in practice tend to be rustic farmhouse with sleek ultra-modern, or very ornate traditional with stark minimalism. They can be done, but they need a very strong unifying element — usually a consistent colour palette — to keep them from fighting each other.

Pro Tip: When pairing styles, start with the two that share the most in common — usually material or colour — and treat the third or fourth style as an accent rather than an equal partner. Let one style dominate at about 60%, the second at 30%, and accent styles at 10%.

How to Use a Consistent Colour Palette to Unify Clashing Furniture Styles

Colour is genuinely the most powerful unifying tool you have when mixing multiple interior design styles. A consistent palette can make a Victorian armchair and a 1970s arc floor lamp look completely intentional together. Without it, even beautifully individual pieces can feel like strangers at a party.

The approach I recommend is what I call the "60-30-10 palette rule" — not a new idea, but one that's particularly useful in mixed-style rooms. Sixty percent of the room is your dominant colour (usually a neutral), thirty percent is a secondary colour (usually a mid-tone), and ten percent is an accent that ties everything together.

How to Build Your Unifying Colour Palette

  • Pull two or three colours from the piece you love most and can't change (often a rug, a sofa or a feature wall).
  • Use those colours as your filter for every other buying decision in the room.
  • Repeat each palette colour at least three times in the room — in art, cushions, decor objects, plant pots.
  • Use your accent colour on at least one piece of wall art or wall decor so the walls feel connected to the room below.
  • If two furniture pieces are fighting each other, add a cushion or throw in a colour that appears in both — it acts as a visual translator.

Here's a fix I use all the time: I had a client with a deep navy velvet sofa and a warm oak mid-century coffee table that felt completely at odds. We added a warm-toned abstract print that had both dusty navy and amber in it, two terracotta cushions on the sofa and a small amber glass vase on the table. That's all it took. Same furniture, completely different feel.

Pro Tip: If you're stuck on your palette, take your phone to each room and photograph it. View the photos in black and white. If the values (lights and darks) feel balanced in greyscale, the room has a good tonal structure regardless of which colours are fighting. If it looks patchy or too dark in one corner, that's where your colour balance needs work.

Common Mixing Mistakes to Avoid and How to Fix Them

The mistakes I see most often in mixed-style rooms are remarkably consistent — and the good news is they're all fixable without starting again from scratch. Most of them come down to a few specific missteps that are easy to spot once you know what to look for.

I'll be honest: I've made a couple of these mistakes myself in rooms I've styled early in my career. The "too many focal points" problem in particular caught me out in a client's bedroom where I was genuinely delighted with every individual piece — and then we stepped back and realised the room looked like an auction house.

Common Mistakes and Their Fixes

  • Mistake: Too many focal points. Fix: Choose one hero element per room and subordinate everything else to it.
  • Mistake: Mixing too many metal finishes. Fix: Pick two finishes maximum — one warm, one dark — and repeat them consistently.
  • Mistake: Scale inconsistency. Fix: Ensure your largest pieces are genuinely large and your small pieces genuinely small — avoid the mid-sized "nothing" zone.
  • Mistake: Art that doesn't connect to the room. Fix: Choose art that contains at least one colour from your room palette.
  • Mistake: All styles equally weighted. Fix: Let one style dominate and use others as accents. A 60/30/10 split always reads as more intentional.
  • Mistake: Ignoring the floor. Fix: Your rug is effectively the ground on which all styles meet — treat it as a unifier, not an afterthought.
  • Mistake: Bare walls in an eclectic room. Fix: In a mixed-style space, bare walls don't read as minimal — they read as unfinished. Even one piece of considered wall art changes this entirely.
Real Example: The mistake I always see with gallery walls in mixed-style rooms is mixing too many frame colours. Gold, black, white and natural wood all in one arrangement is a lot to manage. Choose one frame colour — I usually recommend matte black or natural oak — and let the art itself be the variety. You'll get all the eclectic energy with none of the chaos.

More About Mixing Interior Design Styles the Right Way

Understanding the history and logic behind how different design eras interact helps you make bolder, more confident decisions when blending aesthetics.

One thing I find genuinely useful to remind clients is that mixing styles has always been the norm, not the exception, in well-loved homes. Historically, homes accumulated pieces across decades — a grandmother's armchair here, a contemporary lamp there — and it was the sense of personal history that made them feel alive. The design world's push towards "complete looks" is a relatively recent commercial idea, not a design principle. If you want to go deeper on how different design eras can be combined thoughtfully, This Is the Correct Way to Mix Design Eras is a really solid read that backs this up with practical examples.

The most important thing I'd add is that mixing styles successfully is a skill you develop with practice, not something that has to be perfect from the first attempt. Start with one room, get that feeling right, and let the confidence carry you forward.

WATCH: Master the Art of Mixing Interior Design Styles

Ready to Make Your Mixed-Style Home Work for You?

If there's one thing I hope you take away from all of this, it's that loving multiple interior design styles is not a problem to solve — it's actually a real advantage. The most interesting homes I've ever walked into have always been the ones that reflect a genuine human being with real, layered tastes, not a showroom built around a single aesthetic.

Start small. Pick one room, identify your two dominant styles, find your unifying colour and choose one piece of wall art that bridges them. You don't have to transform the whole house this weekend.

So tell me — which two styles are you trying to bring together right now, and what's the one piece in your room that you absolutely refuse to get rid of? I'd love to hear what you're working with.

Console tables for Japandi design work best when they combine the clean lines of Scandinavian minimalism with the warmth and craftsmanship of Japanese aesthetics — think natural wood, slender legs, a low profile, and absolutely nothing unnecessary on the surface. The right piece grounds your entryway or living room in calm without looking sparse or cold.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in your hallway, staring at a console table that just doesn't feel right — too bulky, too shiny, too "nothing" — and wondered what on earth would actually suit the calm, intentional look you're going for? I ask because I've been there myself, and so have most of my clients. The answer almost always lives at the intersection of considered furniture choice and the wall art and decor you arrange around it.

Quick answer: Japandi console tables are typically low-profile, made from natural wood (like oak, ash or walnut), and styled with minimal clutter. Pair them with neutral-toned wall art, a single ceramic piece, and soft organic textiles to complete the look without overdoing it.

Japandi is a design philosophy that blends the best of Japanese wabi-sabi living — the beauty of imperfection, natural materials, and quiet restraint — with the hygge-influenced cosiness and functionality of Scandinavian interiors. It's one of the most liveable, genuinely calming styles you can bring into a home, and a console table is often the first piece that sets the tone. If you want to pull the full look together, pairing your furniture with unique wall art and thoughtfully chosen unique home decor makes all the difference between a vignette that works and one that just sort of sits there.

What Are Japandi Console Tables?

A Japandi console table is any narrow, flat-topped table that follows the core principles of Japandi design: natural materials, clean geometry, low-to-mid height, and no decorative excess. The look is minimal but never cold — there's always something tactile or organic about it.

What separates a Japandi piece from a generic Scandi one is the attention to craft. Joints might be slightly visible, the grain of the wood is meant to be appreciated, and the overall proportions feel considered rather than simply modern.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A light-filled Japanese-Scandinavian entryway with a low solid-oak console table on slender tapered legs, bare except for a single round ceramic bowl and a small dried-pampas arrangement. Behind it, a raw plaster wall with a wooden wall shelf holding a small woven basket. The floor is pale wide-board timber. A South Asian woman in her thirties stands beside the table, casually arranging the ceramic bowl in a natural candid pose, wearing a soft beige linen outfit.]]

Core Characteristics of a Japandi Console Table

  • Natural solid wood — oak, walnut, ash or bamboo preferred
  • Slender tapered or straight legs, often with visible joinery
  • Low-to-mid height (typically 75–85 cm)
  • Minimal or zero ornamentation
  • Matte or oil-rubbed finishes, never high gloss
  • Occasional open lower shelf for a single decorative object
  • Neutral or warm-toned colour — no painted bright colours
Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether a console table reads as Japandi, turn it around in your mind: would it look at home in a Japanese tea house AND a Danish living room? If yes, you're on the right track.

How To Choose a Japandi Console Table

Choosing the right console table for Japandi design comes down to four things: material, proportion, finish, and how it relates to the wall behind it. Get those right and the rest of the styling becomes much easier.

I always tell clients to measure the wall width before anything else. A console that's too wide makes the space feel squeezed; too narrow and it floats awkwardly. A good rule is 60–75% of the wall width for an entryway, slightly more relaxed for a living room.

[[IMG|how-to-choose-japandi-console-table|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top, then a clear VISUAL comparison (two labelled photos side by side, or simple labelled icons/steps), minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks. Show a side-by-side comparison: LEFT side labelled "Good Japandi Fit" showing a slender oak console with tapered legs, matte finish, and minimal styling; RIGHT side labelled "Not Japandi" showing a heavy dark-stained ornate console with carved details and glossy finish. Add four bullet labels pointing to the key differences: material, leg style, finish, and height proportion.]]

What to Look For When Buying

  • Material: Solid wood beats veneers every time — look for oak, walnut or ash
  • Leg style: Tapered, square or hairpin legs all work; avoid turned or carved ornate legs
  • Height: Match roughly to a standard door handle height or slightly lower
  • Width: Leave at least 20 cm breathing room on each side from the wall edge
  • Finish: Oiled, waxed or natural — avoid lacquered or high-sheen finishes
  • Storage: A single lower shelf adds function without visual clutter
  • Joinery: Visible dovetail or mortise joints are a bonus — they signal quality craft

I once helped a client who'd bought a beautiful walnut console — genuinely lovely piece — but it sat 95 cm tall, which is quite high for the low-ceilinged Victorian hallway she had. It made the whole space feel top-heavy. We swapped it for a lower ash alternative and the hall immediately breathed. Height really does matter more than people realise.

Pro Tip: If you're shopping in person, bring a swatch of your wall colour or flooring. Japandi relies on tonal harmony — a wood that clashes with your floor will fight the whole scheme no matter how beautiful it is on its own.

Styling Your Japandi Console Table

Styling a Japandi console table is about restraint with intention — every object on the surface should earn its place, and there should be noticeable negative space (empty surface) as part of the composition. This is where most people go wrong: they fill it up because empty space feels unfinished. It isn't.

Think in odd numbers and vary the heights of objects. A low ceramic vase, a mid-height candle or twig arrangement, and a trailing plant at one end create a natural diagonal rhythm that draws the eye without overwhelming.

Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A styled Japandi console table in a living room corner, topped with three objects: a short round stoneware vase with a single dried stem, a beeswax pillar candle on a flat stone holder, and a small trailing pothos plant in a terracotta pot at one end. The surface is mostly clear. A simple woven wall sconce hangs above. A Black British woman in her late twenties crouches slightly to adjust the plant, candid and natural, wearing a cream oversized knit.]]

The Japandi Console Styling Formula

  • Keep at least 50% of the surface clear — negative space is intentional, not lazy
  • Use three objects maximum: one low, one mid, one taller or trailing
  • Stick to natural textures: stone, ceramic, linen, dried botanicals, unvarnished wood
  • Avoid anything reflective, metallic or brightly coloured on the surface
  • Add one living element — a plant or fresh stem — to bring warmth and life
  • A small tray in natural rattan or slate keeps keys and everyday items contained
  • Soft ambient lighting via a slim table lamp ties the vignette together after dark
[[PRODUCT|small ceramic stoneware vase for Japandi console decor]]
Real Example: A client of mine tried to style her console with five objects and it looked cluttered. We removed two, shifted the remaining three to the left-hand two-thirds of the surface, and suddenly it looked intentional and calm. The lesson? Edit harder than you think you need to.

Japandi Console Table Variations and Features

Not all Japandi console tables are identical — there's actually a useful range of variations depending on your storage needs, room size, and personal lean towards the Scandi or Japanese end of the aesthetic. Knowing the differences helps you choose a piece that genuinely works for your home rather than just looking pretty on a website.

The most common variation is the shelf console — a single low open shelf below the main surface. It's brilliant for a hallway because you can store a basket of scarves there or a pair of slippers without breaking the visual calm of the top surface.

Pro Tip: If your hallway is narrower than 120 cm, go for a wall-mounted floating console. It gives you the look without eating into the walking space — and it makes the floor feel longer.

Wall Art and Decor Pairings Above a Japandi Console Table

The wall above your console table is genuinely as important as the table itself — possibly more so. It's the first thing the eye travels to when you walk into a room, and if it's bare or wrong, even a perfect console table will feel unfinished.

For Japandi, the wall above should be calm and considered. Think one strong piece of art rather than a gallery wall, a single mirror with a simple frame, or an organic wall-hanging. Busy gallery walls are firmly in the maximalist camp and will undercut the whole aesthetic.

A Japanese-style ceramic bowl and a dried botanical stem sit on the console surface. A woman of East Asian heritage in her forties stands slightly to the side, glancing up at the mirror arrangement with a relaxed thoughtful expression, wearing a sage linen shirt.]]

Best Wall Art and Decor Options for a Japandi Console

  • Abstract botanical prints — ink-wash or watercolour styles in earth tones or sumi-e (Japanese ink) look outstanding
  • Single large-format art print — one piece, centred, roughly two-thirds the width of the console below it
  • Round or arch-top mirror — adds light and softness without visual noise
  • Woven macramé or tapestry panel — textural, organic, very much in keeping with wabi-sabi
  • Simple wooden wall shelf above — hold a single object and leave space around it
  • Wall-mounted branch or dried botanical — brings nature indoors in the most pared-back way
  • Framed calligraphy or kanji-style text art — if kept to one piece in black on cream, it's quietly beautiful

The most common mistake I see here is hanging the art too high. I visited a client's flat once where a lovely abstract print was hung almost at ceiling height above the console — it looked like it was floating away from everything below it. Dropped it down so the bottom of the frame sat about 25 cm above the console surface and the whole vignette clicked into place immediately.

[[PRODUCT|abstract botanical wall art prints in earth tones for Japandi styling]] [[PRODUCT|Japanese ink-wash landscape artwork for entryway wall]]
Pro Tip: When choosing art for above a console table, aim for the bottom of the frame to sit roughly 20–30 cm above the table surface. Any higher and the art disconnects from the furniture below; any lower and it feels cramped.

Colour Palette Guidance for Japandi Entryway Vignettes

Getting the colour palette right is honestly what separates a convincing Japandi entryway from one that just has a wooden table in it. The palette is deceptively simple — but there's more going on than pure white and beige.

Japandi colour sits in a narrow band: warm off-whites, stone, clay, sage, charcoal, dusty terracotta, and the natural tones of wood and linen. What you're avoiding is anything that shouts — no bright whites, no saturated colours, no cool greys without warmth in them.

Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A Japandi entryway styled in a warm palette of stone, clay and warm off-white. Walls are clay-lime plaster, the console is ash wood with a natural oil finish. A terracotta ceramic pot with a green trailing plant sits at one end of the console. A round jute wall hanging adds texture to the wall. A Middle Eastern man in his fifties stands near the console, hands in pockets, looking relaxed and at ease in the space, wearing a soft charcoal linen jacket.]]

Japandi Entryway Colour Palette by Layer

  • Wall colour: Warm off-white, raw plaster tone, pale stone or dusty sage — avoid cool or blue-toned whites
  • Floor: Pale to mid-tone timber, natural stone tiles, or warm-toned concrete
  • Console wood tone: Light ash or oak for a Scandi lean; darker walnut for a more Japanese feel
  • Accent colours: One or two only — muted terracotta, dusty sage or deep charcoal
  • Art and textiles: Cream, warm white, tan, sand, ink black — echo the wall and wood tones
  • Avoid: Bright white walls, cool grey tones, navy, mustard or any saturated colour
Real Example: I worked with a couple who'd painted their hallway a stark brilliant white, then wondered why their beautiful oak console looked slightly cold. We repainted in a warm stone-white — just a touch of yellow and grey in the pigment — and the wood suddenly looked alive. The room hadn't changed; the background had.

Budget vs Premium Japandi Console Table Options

Here's something I appreciate about Japandi design: the aesthetic actually rewards restraint in budget as much as it rewards craftsmanship at the higher end. You genuinely don't need to spend a fortune if you know what to prioritise.

The key is knowing where to invest and where to save. I'd always put money into the table itself over the styling objects — a well-made solid wood piece will outlast trends and take on a better patina over time. The decor around it can be budget-friendly and still look curated.

[[IMG|budget-vs-premium-japandi-console|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top, then a clear VISUAL comparison (two labelled photos side by side, or simple labelled icons/steps), minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks. Show a two-column comparison: LEFT column titled "Budget Japandi Console Setup" with a simple pine or rubberwood console illustration and three budget styling objects (ceramic bowl, dried stem, small basket); RIGHT column titled "Premium Japandi Console Setup" with a solid walnut console illustration and three quality styling objects (handmade ceramic, sculptural vessel, woven rattan tray). Below each column add total approximate cost ranges as text labels.]]

Where to Spend vs Where to Save

  • Spend on: Solid wood table, quality joinery, a well-made piece of wall art above it
  • Save on: Ceramic vessels from supermarkets or charity shops, dried botanicals from a florist's offcuts
  • Budget table tip: A plain pine or rubberwood table painted with a chalk-finish paint in a warm neutral reads surprisingly well in Japandi settings
  • Premium table tip: Solid walnut with hand-finished oil and exposed tenon joints is the gold standard — worth the investment if your hallway is a focal space
  • Mid-range sweet spot: Solid oak from Scandinavian furniture chains hits quality without premium pricing
  • Art investment: One well-chosen art print above a budget console transforms the whole vignette — this is worth spending on
[[PRODUCT|minimalist Japandi wall art print for entryway styling]]
Pro Tip: If budget is tight, start with a solid secondhand table from a vintage market — older Scandi furniture from the 60s and 70s is practically Japandi-ready as it is — and invest in one quality piece of art for the wall above it. That combination will look far more intentional than a cheap new table with a bare wall.

DIY Japandi Console Table Styling Tips with Accessible Decor

You don't need a stylist's budget or access to niche design boutiques to create a convincing Japandi console vignette. Most of the best pieces in this look are things you can find in garden centres, charity shops, supermarkets, or even in your own garden.

I've done entire console table setups for clients using items that cost less than twenty pounds total, and they've photographed beautifully. The trick is always in the edit — choosing a few genuinely nice things and giving them space to breathe rather than crowding the surface.

[[IMG|diy-japandi-console-styling-accessible|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A DIY Japandi console table styled with accessible items: a supermarket ceramic mug repurposed as a vase holding a single eucalyptus stem, a flat river pebble as a candle holder, and a folded beige linen cloth draped at one end. The table is a simple pale wood piece. A hanging plant in a macramé hanger is visible on the wall above. A young woman of mixed British-Caribbean heritage crouches beside the table, arranging a small stem in the ceramic vessel with a focused, relaxed expression.]]

DIY Styling Sources and Swaps

  • Vessels: Plain supermarket ceramic mugs, jars, or small bowls work beautifully as vases — choose cream, terracotta or stone tones
  • Botanicals: Dried pampas, eucalyptus, or even garden twigs in winter add organic texture for almost nothing
  • Trays: A piece of flat slate, a chopping board, or a folded linen cloth corrals smaller items tidily
  • Candles: Cream beeswax pillar candles from food shops or pound stores hit the Japandi palette perfectly
  • Wall decor: A large round mirror from a charity shop, spray-painted matte black or left natural, reads as intentional
  • Plants: A single pothos, spider plant or small olive tree in a terracotta pot is Japandi at its most honest
  • Art: Print a botanical ink-wash image at home in black and white and frame it in a simple raw wood frame
[[PRODUCT|wabi-sabi style nature wall art prints for budget Japandi styling]] [[PRODUCT|woven jute or rattan decorative tray for console table]]
Pro Tip: The single most accessible DIY upgrade for a Japandi console is a plain terracotta pot with a trailing plant, placed at one end of the surface. It costs a few pounds, brings life and warmth, and immediately makes the arrangement feel intentional rather than accidental.

Japandi Console Table Looks and Style Inspiration

Sometimes the easiest way to pull a look together is to see it in action across a few different interpretations. Here are some of the most compelling real-world Japandi console styles — from the very stripped back to the slightly warmer and more layered.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Japandi Home Decor Trend - serene minimalist Japanese Scandinavian fusion
  • Scandi Home Decor Trend - clean lines functional Nordic simplicity
  • Zen Room Decoration Trend - calm balanced mindful interior spaces

What the Experts Say About Japandi Design

Japandi has moved well beyond trend status — it's becoming one of the defining residential interior styles of the decade, and it's easy to see why when you understand what it's actually doing for people's sense of calm at home.

The philosophy at its heart is about reducing visual noise without reducing warmth. That's the balance that makes Japandi so liveable compared to pure minimalism, which can feel cold and aspirational in a way that's exhausting to maintain day to day.

If you want to read more about the history and principles behind the style, Japandi Style: Everything You Need to Know About These East-Meets-West Interiors from Architectural Digest is a genuinely useful deep read — it explains the wabi-sabi and hygge connections in a way that gives you real context for your decor decisions.

The practical upshot for console table styling is this: Japandi design rewards permanence over trend-chasing. The table, the art above it, the ceramic on the surface — buy these things carefully and they'll work just as well in fifteen years as they do today.

WATCH: Genius Japandi Console Table Ideas That Blend Industrial Edge with Natural Calm Minimalism

Let's Keep the Conversation Going

Creating a Japandi console table vignette really is one of the most satisfying things you can do for a home — it's focused, achievable, and the result is a corner of your space that genuinely feels considered and calm every single day you walk past it.

Whether you're starting from scratch with a new table or working with something you already own, the principles are the same: natural materials, a restrained surface, one strong piece on the wall above, and a palette that borrows warmth from wood and nature rather than from colour.

You don't need to do it all at once either. Start with the table and one object. Then add the art. Then refine from there. The best Japandi spaces I've ever seen were built slowly over time, not installed in a weekend.

So — what does your current entryway or console table situation look like, and what's the one thing you'd most like to change about it first?

The console surface holds just three objects: a round stoneware bowl, a dried botanical stem in a simple ceramic vessel, and a small trailing plant in a terracotta pot at one end. Above the console, a large round rattan mirror is centred on the wall. The floor is pale wide-board timber. The overall palette is warm stone, ash wood, cream and dusty terracotta. No framed wall art on the walls. The scene is calm, lived-in, and quietly beautiful — not staged or perfect.
